items.text: With reference to the data above and your knowledge of economics, evaluate whether Air India is likely to benefit from privatisation.
items.answer:
AO2 (4 marks)/AO3 (4 marks)/AO4 (4 marks) 
AO2 and AO3 
● Privatisation involves the sale of state-owned resources to the private 
sector 
● The Indian Government wants to sell the airline Air India to private 
investors 
● This means that the airline would no longer be controlled by the 
government and would be more likely to pursue different objectives, such 
as making a profit 
● It may mean Air India would be more likely to reverse the current loss and 
to be able to pay for its fuel 
● Private investors may bring increased investment to the airline, meaning it 
is able to offer increased flights to destinations in countries in Africa and 
the rest of Asia 
● This would increase Air India’s competitiveness with other airlines already 
flying to a higher number of destinations 
● Therefore, this would complement a new objective to make a profit 
● This is more likely to be achievable as the new owner(s) may have more 
experience and skills in managing an airline than the government 
AO4 
● However, the Indian Government has reduced the debt faced by Air India in 
the past and therefore could leave the airline struggling to meet its costs 
without assistance from the state 
● There is already a lot of competition from other airlines meaning the 
changes may not lead to benefits for Air India; it may be out of the airline’s 
control 
● As oil companies have struggled to receive payment for fuel in the past, 
they may be reluctant to supply the firm, even with new owners 
● This could mean that Air India needs to prioritise different objectives before 
looking to make a profit and/or establish new routes 
● It may depend on the level of investment from the new private owner(s) as 
well as their personal objectives 
● In the short term it may be more difficult for Air India to make a profit but 
this may be easier in the long term if the private owner(s) can use their 
skills and experience to the benefit of the airline

items.text: With reference to the data above and your knowledge of economics, assess the likely effectiveness of the tourist tax in dealing with negative externalities, such as overcrowding.
items.answer:
AO2 (3 marks)/AO3 (3 marks)/AO4 (3 marks) 
AO2 and AO3 
• Negative externalities are spillover effects on third parties due to 
consumption/production 
• Overcrowding in Venice may cause pollution, litter and congestion issues for 
residents and other visitors 
• One method of government intervention to reduce negative externalities is 
the use of taxation 
• A tourist tax is a compulsory financial charge made by the government on 
individuals 
• A tourist tax would make it more expensive to visit Venice 
• Therefore, it is likely to reduce the number of tourists in Venice from the 
estimated 24 million who visit each year 
• The higher the tourist tax, the fewer tourists there are likely to be, meaning 
at its highest charge of €10, the reduction should be greatest 
• As a result, the negative externality, such as overcrowding, may be reduced 
AO4 
• However, as Venice is so popular, some tourists may decide it is worth 
paying the tourist tax 
• This may especially be the case at the lower rates of tourist tax, where a 
tourist may not consider €3 unaffordable compared to the price of their trip 
• It takes time to collect the tourist tax, meaning there may be more 
congestion when people arrive in Venice 
• Even a reduction in numbers may not be enough to deal with the 
externalities caused by the high number of visitors each year 
• Those visitors who are prepared to pay the tourist tax will be generating 
revenue for the city which may be used to help combat the externalities in 
other ways 
• Other methods of government intervention may be more effective

items.text: With reference to the data above and your knowledge of economics, evaluate whether introducing division of labour is the best way for Raphael to increase productivity in his pastry-making factory.
items.answer:
AO2 (4 marks)/AO3 (4 marks)/AO4 (4 marks) 
AO2 and AO3 
• 
Division of labour means dividing the production process into different 
stages where each worker specialises in one task 
• 
Productivity is the amount of output that can be produced in a period of 
time, with a given quantity of resources 
• 
Division of labour leads to less time being wasted as workers will not have 
to switch between different parts of production such as mixing 
ingredients and shaping the dough 
• 
This means the employees at the pastry-making factory can become more 
productive as they are able to develop skills in the task they perform, 
becoming more specialised 
• 
This may be particularly important in order for Raphael’s factory to meet 
demand from the restaurants and street vendors in Madrid, to whom it 
sells 
• 
It can be easier to integrate machinery into the production process as the 
tasks are broken down into different stages 
AO4 
• 
However, the pastry-making factory employees may find doing the same 
task, such as combining the cooled mixture with egg, very boring and 
monotonous 
• 
This could mean they lose concentration and may make mistakes, leading 
to a lower rate of productivity 
• 
Therefore, a delay in supplying the pastry for churros to restaurants and 
street vendors in Madrid could occur and lead to a loss of business for the 
factory 
• 
This is especially likely as the restaurants are busy and may be unable to 
meet their own customer’s demand for churros without the pastry 
• 
Improving the quality of labour by training employees to use pastry-
making equipment could increase productivity more, as could investing in 
more advanced facilities with which to bake 
• 
It depends whether the pastry-making tasks require much training as they 
maybe more suited to the division of labour process 
• 
Raphael could introduce rotation of tasks to reduce the monotony or use 
division of labour alongside other factors, such as advanced baking 
facilities

items.text: A worker’s education level is likely to affect their ability in the workplace. When a person migrates to another country, they bring their knowledge, skills and information. With reference to the data and your knowledge of economics, assess the importance of the quality of labour on productivity in a country.
items.answer:
AO2 (3 marks)/AO3 (3 marks)/AO4 (3 marks) 
AO2 and AO3 
• Quality of labour may increase as a result of education because workers would 
be able to develop skills with which they could become more efficient in the 
tasks needed to produce goods and services in the workplace 
• Therefore, workers are likely to be able to produce more goods and services in a 
shorter period of time, leading to lower costs of production for firms 
• This increase in productivity means that a firm may be able to enjoy higher 
profits due to lower costs, as well as a possible increase in revenue, if more 
products are available to sell 
• An increase in immigration may lead to an increase in the quantity and quality 
of labour supplied 
• This may result in increased competition between workers to provide the most 
efficient labour to firms in order to reduce their costs of production 
• This may mean that some workers may aim to increase their education to 
become more productive 
AO4 
• However, it takes time for education to become effective as periods of study 
need to be completed before being used in the workplace 
• This means that education may only impact productivity at a later date, making 
it difficult to measure its impact 
• Skilled workers may emigrate, taking their ability to increase efficiency for a 
firm with them 
• Immigration which increases the supply of skilled labour may lead to a 
reduction in wages, potentially demotivating workers and discouraging 
productivity 
• Therefore, productivity may not always increase due to quality of labour, at 
least not in the short-run 
• It may depend on the country and the levels of productivity within it or on 
technological advances in capital or land use

items.text: Twitter was bought for $44bn by Elon Musk in 2022. His aim includes creating an “everything app” for messaging, payments, ridesharing, food delivery and more; Twitter was renamed X. Users rose to 530 million by 2023 after publicity about the name change, reducing the need for high advertising expenditure. Advanced technology and research and development will enable multiple functions but are likely to be costly. Advertising revenue has fallen by 65%, and thousands of workers, including managers, have lost their jobs. With reference to the data and your knowledge of economics, evaluate whether X is likely to benefit from economies of scale.
items.answer:
AO2 (4 marks)/AO3 (4 marks)/AO4 (4 marks) 
AO2 and AO3 
• The number of users of the newly named X increased to a new high of 530 
million people within the first year 
• This means that the (long-run) average costs are likely to be reduced 
because they are spread over a larger number of users 
• By creating a platform that enables users to perform multiple tasks, such as 
messaging, making payments and having food delivered, fewer resources 
would be needed, leading to lower (long-term) average costs (technical 
economies) 
• The cost of developing the advanced technology may be lower for X, as a 
substantial amount of research/components are likely to be required, 
possibly leading to purchasing economies 
• Due to the increase in size, managerial economies may be present as 
specialist managers could oversee separate functions of X, bringing in 
specialist expertise and lowering (long-run) average costs 
• (Long-run) average costs could also be reduced as all tasks could be 
advertised together, therefore spreading the marketing costs and allowing 
marketing economies to take place 
• The takeover cost of $44bn suggests the platform is extremely large, 
therefore, financial economies are likely because it should be able to get 
access to money more cheaply than a smaller firm, including to 
purchase/develop the advanced technology 
AO4 
• If a firm grows too large, average costs are likely to rise due to diseconomies 
of scale 
• The loss of around 65% advertising revenue may reduce X’s ability to create 
the platform envisaged by Elon Musk 
• Thousands of workers lost their jobs as a result of the purchase by Elon 
Musk, meaning a decrease in efficiency of remaining workers may be likely 
if they are worried about losing their jobs too 
• This means diseconomies of scale may occur as the average costs may 
increase due to less productive workers 
• The renaming of the platform from Twitter to X, alongside other major 
changes may cause further issues for X, such as workers being demotivated 
• Communication problems and a lack of control may be caused by having 
such a large firm trying to integrate resources. As the platform relies on 
technology being used effectively, this may lead to diseconomies of scale 
• As the combined number of users is already more than 530 million, the 
platform may have already reached the most efficient point and the lowest 
(long-run) average cost 
• It will take time for the technology to be successfully implemented and so 
economies of scale may not occur for several years 
• If users do not agree/like the changes they may move to a competitor 
• Workers may actually be more productive due to the high number of job 
losses, as they want to prove worthy of keeping employment. This could 
help to lower average costs 
• It may take time to understand the implications of the changes for X and 
whether economies or diseconomies of scale occur will therefore depend 
on the outcome

items.text: Fitnation is a fitness centre in Almaty, Kazakhstan, offering activities including boxing. It aims to do charitable work by giving city residents access to boxing facilities and coaching at a discounted price one day a week, making it more accessible to people who otherwise could not afford it. However, its facilities are very busy that day, reducing availability for members paying the full monthly price of $25–$50. With reference to this data and your knowledge of economics, assess the benefits to Fitnation of offering the discounted price.

customers, completing charitable work or maximising revenue/sales 
 As Fitnation regularly offers discounted entry to city residents, 
making a profit is not its main aim 
 Instead, the aim could be described as completing charitable work,

 This is because they cannot make the most of their membership and 
the money they paid, so they are not able to maximise their benefit 
 Therefore, the number of members/people paying full price to 
access the facilities at the fitness centre may decrease

items.text: In January 2025, Western Australia announced AU$107m investment to expand the 72 km Swan River ferry network. Five new electric ferries, built by local firms, can carry over 130 passengers each; two stops would connect to a bus depot and the University of Western Australia. Local sailing clubs raised safety concerns, while opponents warned extra ferry-user parking could cause problems. With reference to this data and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the extent to which public-sector investment may benefit Western Australia’s economy.
items.answer:
AO2 (4 marks)/AO3 (4 marks)/AO4 (4 marks)
AO2 and AO3 
 The public sector is a part of the economy which is owned by the 
government and operates in the public interest 
 An investment of AU$107m would greatly improve the Swan River 
ferry network, by increasing the number of ferries and stops along 
the river 
 This means there would be greater capacity to transport 
passengers (>130 people per ferry trip), connecting more people 
across the Perth area 
 Therefore, it may be easier/more accessible for people to work in 
more locations in Perth than without the increase in infrastructure 
 A greater number and variety of jobs is likely to be available both 
during the building and operation of the additional ferries 
 This would create a positive effect for local firms and may 
increase more revenue for the Western Australia Government 
through tax 
 Instead of causing a parking issue, the investment may reduce 
traffic, as the new stops would allow passengers to travel more 
easily by buses connecting with the ferries and/or access to 
university without using private transport 
AO4 
 However, the cost of expanding the ferry network means the 
Western Australian Government would have less revenue 
available for spending on health and education 
 Therefore, the economy of Western Australia may not benefit as 
much from public sector investment to improve the network as if 
the AU$107m was invested elsewhere 
 This may be intensified if parking by ferry users leads to 
accidents and/or congestion due to the increased usage 
 It will most likely take time for the building of new ferries and 
addition of new stops, meaning any benefit may not be seen for 
a number of years 
 Therefore, costs may be considerably higher than revenue, for 
the government and the economy during this time 
 Safety concerns have been raised, meaning additional spending 
may be needed to investigate potential dangers to small boat 
users and to rectify problems

items.text: Foxconn Technology produces Apple’s new iPhone at its Shenzhen factory in China, employing 270,000 workers, each performing a specific task from screen handling and assembly to checking and packaging. With reference to the data and your knowledge of economics, assess the benefits to Foxconn Technology of using division of labour.
items.answer: AO2 (3 marks)/AO3 (3 marks)/AO4 (3 marks). AO2/AO3: division of labour breaks production into smaller tasks; each worker specialises (for example handling the screen, checking the phone or packaging it); specialisation can make work faster and more accurate, increasing productivity and reducing Foxconn’s production costs. Workers avoid time lost switching tasks. AO4: repetitive iPhone tasks may bore workers and reduce motivation, causing mistakes, rework, lower productivity and higher costs. A failure at one production stage can halt later stages; this risk may matter with 270,000 workers and many divided tasks. Specialisation may also create problems when a worker is absent and no replacement has the required skill. Level guidance: 1–3 basic/limited and one-sided; 4–6 partial analysis with more than one view but potentially unbalanced; 7–9 clear applied analysis and a balanced, coherent evaluation.

items.text: Dubai has a population of over 2.5 million; immigrant workers make up over 80% of the population, many in construction, cleaning or care. With reference to the data and your knowledge of economics, assess the benefits to Dubai of employing such a high proportion of migrant labour.
items.answer: AO2 (3 marks)/AO3 (3 marks)/AO4 (3 marks). AO2/AO3: migration is movement to live in a foreign country; migrant workers increase labour supply, potentially shifting labour supply right, increasing employment and reducing shortages. Dubai’s 2 million migrants (80% of the population), including construction workers, make a large contribution to labour supply and may support productivity and economic expansion. AO4: most migrants work in construction, cleaning and care, so other sectors may still lack workers; migrants may not have the required skills and supply may be short-term if they return home. Raising the retirement age, lowering the school-leaving age or enabling more women to work may offer a more effective long-term or cross-sector labour supply. Level guidance: 1–3 basic/limited and one-sided; 4–6 partial analysis and potentially unbalanced; 7–9 clear applied analysis and balanced evaluation.

items.text: In Poland, obesity has increased. Consumers of sugary drinks such as Coca-Cola and Fanta pay an additional 0.50 zloty ($0.11) per litre after a sugar tax; advertising has also increased, and consumers continue buying the drinks despite the higher price. With reference to the data and your knowledge of economics, analyse why consumers may not maximise their benefit when consuming sugary drinks.
items.answer: AO2 (3 marks)/AO3 (3 marks). Consumers may not calculate what is best for them; increased advertising can pressure them to buy unhealthy products. Consumers may lack full information about the negative effects of sugar in drinks such as Coca Cola and Fanta. Habits and taste can make behaviour difficult to change; consumers may continue buying despite the extra 0.50 zloty ($0.11) per litre, especially if it is a small share of income. Friends’ consumption may also influence consumers to copy the behaviour. Level guidance: 1–2 basic/limited; 3–4 partial application and some analysis; 5–6 clear application and thorough analysis.

items.text: NT Massage is a successful family-run Hong Kong business serving long-standing local customers. Mei wants to expand into a chain in busier areas, train employees, advertise in hotels and attract tourists and business people among Hong Kong’s 7.5 million population; many similar businesses compete. With reference to the data and your knowledge of economics, evaluate whether the family should expand rather than keep the business small.
items.answer: AO2 (4 marks)/AO3 (4 marks)/AO4 (4 marks). AO2/AO3: expansion may serve more customers and increase profit; NT Massage could charge higher prices in busier locations, attract tourists and business people, increase revenue, spread risk beyond its current residential location, gain access to finance and benefit from economies of scale such as spreading advertising costs. AO4: expansion could weaken the traditional service valued by long-standing customers; coordinating several shops may create diseconomies of scale for a family used to one shop; competitors may make custom difficult to attract; growth takes time and money, delays profit and may strain the existing business. The judgement may depend on competitors, successful advertising and tourism/business demand. Level guidance: 1–4 isolated/basic, limited development, one-sided and unlikely supported judgement; 5–8 some selectivity and development, more than one view but balance/support may be limited; 9–12 specific, accurate, coherent applied analysis, balanced evaluation and supported judgement.
